## Proof

**Claim:** Yes. Given any finite integer sequence $(x_1, \dots, x_N)$, $x_i \in \mathbb{Z}$, there exists $f \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ with $f(i) = x_i$ for $i = 1, \dots, N$ and $\lim_{x \to \pm\infty} f(x) = 0$.

**Construction.** Let $\phi: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the standard smooth bump function

$$
\phi(x) = \begin{cases} \exp\!\Big(\dfrac{-1}{1 - x^2}\Big), & |x| < 1, \\[6pt] 0, & |x| \ge 1. \end{cases}
$$

It is well known (and verified by induction on derivatives at $x = \pm 1$) that $\phi \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ and $\operatorname{supp} \phi = [-1, 1]$. Since $\phi(0) = e^{-1} \neq 0$, define the normalized bump

$$
\psi(x) := \frac{\phi(x)}{\phi(0)} = e^{\,1 - \frac{1}{1-x^2}} \text{ for } |x|<1, \quad \psi(x)=0 \text{ for } |x|\ge 1.
$$

Then $\psi \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$, $\operatorname{supp}\psi \subseteq [-1,1]$, and $\psi(0) = 1$.

Now set

$$
\boxed{\,f(x) := \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i\,\psi(x - i).\,}
$$

**Verification of the three required properties.**

1. **Smoothness.** Each summand $x_i\,\psi(x-i)$ is $C^\infty$ (a constant times a translate of a $C^\infty$ function). A finite sum of $C^\infty$ functions is $C^\infty$, so $f \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$.

2. **Interpolation.** For each $j \in \{1, \dots, N\}$,
$$
f(j) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i\,\psi(j - i).
$$
When $i = j$, the argument is $0$, giving $\psi(0) = 1$. When $i \neq j$, the argument is $j - i$, a nonzero integer, hence $|j - i| \ge 1$, so $\psi(j-i) = 0$. Therefore
$$
f(j) = x_j \cdot 1 + \sum_{i \neq j} x_i \cdot 0 = x_j.
$$

3. **Vanishing at infinity.** Each summand has support $\operatorname{supp}\big(x_i\,\psi(\cdot - i)\big) \subseteq [i-1,\, i+1]$. Hence
$$
\operatorname{supp} f \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^{N} [i-1,\, i+1] \subseteq [0,\, N+1],
$$
which is compact. In particular $f \equiv 0$ on $(-\infty, 0) \cup (N+1, \infty)$, so
$$
\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = 0 \quad\text{and}\quad \lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = 0.
$$

**Remark on the note in the problem.** Interpolating polynomials (e.g. Lagrange) generically grow like $|x|^{N-1}$ and thus diverge at $\pm\infty$. The bump-function construction above avoids this entirely because compact support forces decay to zero *exactly*, not merely asymptotically — the function is literally zero outside a bounded interval, while remaining $C^\infty$ everywhere (the "flat" behavior at the boundary of the support is precisely what the $\exp(-1/(1-x^2))$ factor guarantees). $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
